questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Complete a city population balance
questions.stem: A dashboard tile shows a city's population change of 14,200 over ten years and its natural increase of 9,800. Which balance completes the tile?

options.text: A net migration of 4,400, because the natural increase must be added to the population change
options.misconception: adds natural increase when it should subtract it

options.text: A net migration of 4,400, because the change of 14,200 less natural increase of 9,800 leaves 4,400
A net migration of 14,200, because the population change is itself the migration balance
options.misconception: treats the total change as though it were migration alone

options.text: A net migration of 9,800, because natural increase is the only component that changes a population
options.misconception: ignores migration and leaves natural increase as the balance

questions.explanation: The balance closes as change equals natural increase plus net migration, so net migration is 14,200 less 9,800, which is 4,400. Adding the components, or using one of them as the whole balance, doubles the movement or hides it.
questions.hint: Change equals natural increase plus net migration.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effects of remittances on a village
questions.stem: A dashboard note describes an upland village where a third of households receive money from relatives working in coastal cities. Explain what this means for the village's economy and for how its residents might be counted.

answer.exemplar: Remittances inject income that does not come from local production, which can raise consumption, pay for schooling, and smooth seasonal shortfalls without any new local work. For population counting, the money can support the village even when working-age residents are away, so the number of residents present on census night may be lower than the number the village supports, and the income belongs to the household of origin rather than to the destination economy.

questions.explanation: Remittance income replaces local earnings and can keep a village active while its workers are away. It affects counted population, since supported residents may live elsewhere, and it accrues to the sending household.
questions.hint: Ask where the money comes from and who counts.

options.misconception: treats a wide base as if it were the whole dependency measure

The district has an old population, because the median age of 31 is high for a growing district
options.misconception: reads a mid-range median as proof of an ageing population

questions.explanation: The base shows the number of young children only, while a dependency ratio needs the young and the old together. A median of 31 and a ratio of 58 cannot be explained from the base.

Use the total area, because it is the only figure that appears in official statistics

options.misconception: accepts the right denominator but justifies it with a wrong claim

options.text: Use the population as the denominator, because density must always be expressed per person
options.misconception: confuses the numerator with the denominator of a density measure

questions.explanation: Two denominators give two answers for one district, so the choice decides what is compared. Habitable area makes districts with unproductive tracts comparable; total area measures land, not crowding.

options.text: Density and distribution are two names for the same measure expressed in different units
options.misconception: treats two different measures as interchangeable labels

options.misconception: reaches the right figure through faulty reasoning

options.text: 7,700 people, because net migration of 4,500 plus the 3,200 who departed equals gross arrivals
1,300 people, because the 3,200 who left should be subtracted from net migration
options.misconception: subtracts departures when they must be added back

questions.topic: Choosing a denominator for a migration rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain the choice of a migration rate denominator
questions.stem: A dashboard panel offers two migration-rate tiles for the same city and year, one dividing arrivals by the population at the start of the year and one dividing by the mid-year population. Explain why the choice of denominator changes the number and which is preferred.

answer.exemplar: The in-migration rate divides arrivals by the population at risk of moving, which is the mid-year population, because arrivals are spread across the year. Using the population at the start of the year treats the city as if it had been that size for all twelve months, and in a fast-growing city that understates the rate. Reporting the denominator alongside the rate lets a reader see which convention was used and compare districts properly.

questions.explanation: A rate divides a flow by the population it occurred within, and the mid-year population matches a flow spread across a year. A start-of-year base is too small in a growing city and inflates the rate.
questions.hint: Use the population at risk during the period.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Complete a balance and interpret the result
questions.stem: A dashboard shows a city's population rising from 410,000 to 468,000 over twenty years, with natural increase of 74,000. Explain how you complete the balance and what the remaining figure tells you.

answer.exemplar: The change over the period is 58,000, and natural increase accounts for 74,000, so the balance closes with net migration of 16,000 more people leaving than arriving. A negative migration balance of that size over twenty years is a slow, persistent loss rather than a single shock, and it means the city would have grown faster without out-migration.

questions.explanation: Change equals natural increase plus net migration, so 58,000 less 74,000 leaves 16,000 of net out-migration. A balance that stays negative over decades points to sustained outflow rather than a one-off change.
questions.hint: Subtract natural increase from the total change.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identical density hides different patterns
questions.stem: A dashboard compares a coastal district where households cluster in a ribbon along the shore with an inland district where homes scatter evenly across farmland. Explain why the two areas can show identical density figures and still need very different service plans.

answer.exemplar: Density divides population by area, so a ribbon settlement and a scattered one with the same ratio of people to square kilometres produce identical figures. The plans differ because a ribbon concentrates demand along one corridor, so a clinic, a bus route, and a water main must follow the line of settlement, while a scattered district needs multiple small facilities spread widely. The density tile conceals both patterns, which is why a distribution layer has to be read alongside it.

questions.explanation: Identical density figures can hide different settlement patterns, and those patterns decide where services go. A density tile alone cannot guide provision, so a distribution view must accompany it.
questions.hint: Ask how the people are spread, not just how many.

questions.stem: A dashboard must publish two density figures for a district: one over the whole administrative area and one over the land people actually live on. Explain why both can be defensible and what each one is for.

answer.exemplar: The total-area figure is the standard administrative measure and is comparable with national statistics, but it mixes inhabited land with mountains, forest, and water. The habitable-area figure strips that out and gives a truer picture of how crowded the settled part is, which is what matters for housing, schooling, and service planning. Publishing both with the area definitions attached stops readers from treating them as competing measurements of the same thing.

questions.explanation: Total area answers the administrative comparison question; habitable area answers the crowding and planning question. Publishing both, each labelled with the area used, stops readers confusing them.
questions.hint: Ask which question each figure is meant to answer.

questions.learningObjective: Derive an area from a published density
questions.stem: A district's dashboard reports a density of 45 people per square kilometre and a total population of 135,000. What is the total area of the district in square kilometres?
questions.explanation: Density is population over area, so area is population over density: 135,000 divided by 45 gives 3,000 square kilometres. Multiplying instead of dividing gives the wrong units entirely.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Adjust a balance for newly counted residents

stimulus.body: A balance panel for a coastal city shows a population of 780,000, a ten-year change of 62,000, and a natural increase of 88,000. A note explains that the natural increase figure includes 4,000 newborns counted for the first time, who were not present at the earlier count.

questions.stem: Using the balance panel, what does the note imply about the city's migration balance?

options.text: Net out-migration of 26,000, because the change of 62,000 minus natural increase of 88,000 gives the balance
options.misconception: ignores the note about the newly counted newborns

options.text: Net in-migration of 26,000, because the change of 62,000 plus natural increase of 88,000 gives the balance
options.misconception: adds the components of the balance instead of subtracting

options.text: Net out-migration of 30,000, once the 4,000 newly counted newborns are taken out of the change
Net out-migration of 4,000, because the newborns alone explain the whole difference between change and natural increase
options.misconception: treats the note about newborns as the whole of the imbalance

questions.explanation: The change of 62,000 includes 4,000 newly counted people, so the real increase is 58,000, and 58,000 less 88,000 of natural increase leaves 30,000 of net out-migration. Ignoring the note overstates the loss.
questions.hint: Remove the newly counted people from the change first.

options.text: The figure is correct, because 7,560 over 420,000 scales to 18 per 1,000 mid-year residents
The figure is wrong, because departures should be divided by the population at the start of the year
options.misconception: rejects a correct rate by applying an inconsistent rule

options.text: The figure is correct, because any population total is acceptable as the denominator
options.misconception: accepts any denominator without checking the convention

options.text: The figure is wrong, because out-migration rates must be expressed per hundred residents
options.misconception: insists on a per-hundred base for an out-migration rate

questions.explanation: 7,560 over 420,000 scaled by a thousand gives exactly 18 per 1,000, so the tile is right. A rate must state its denominator, and accepting any denominator would make the panel unreliable.
questions.hint: Divide departures by the mid-year population, then scale.

questions.learningObjective: Identify how remittances affect village population

options.misconception: links the delivery mechanism to population change without evidence

options.text: Transfers are sent monthly, so a village's population cannot be affected by them over ten years
options.misconception: thinks regular payments rule out any long-term effect

options.text: Transfers are spent on food, so they keep villagers at home and stop rural to urban movement
options.misconception: assumes spending on food pins people to the village permanently

options.text: Transfers can support households left behind, which may slow the departure of working-age adults

questions.explanation: Where transfers cover a household's costs, family members no longer need to move for work, so out-migration can slow. Details of how money is delivered or spent have no such clear link.

options.text: 40 per cent, because the remittances should be divided by the non-remittance income of 8,000
options.misconception: divides the transfer by income from other sources only

options.text: 20 per cent, because remittances of 2,000 sit inside a total income of 10,000
6.7 per cent, because the remittances should be divided by the sum of all three income sources
options.misconception: reaches a figure that misstates the ratio and its method

options.text: 20 per cent, but only because wages are treated as part of the local economy
options.misconception: gives the right figure with a reason that adds nothing

questions.explanation: Total income is 10,000, so the remittance share is 2,000 over 10,000, or 20 per cent. Dividing by the other sources instead measures how large transfers are, not their share of income.
questions.hint: Add all income sources, then take the share.

questions.topic: Why a pyramid's base cannot stand alone
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of comparing pyramid bases
questions.stem: A dashboard shows pyramids for two districts side by side. One has a broad base and a narrow top; the other has a narrow base and a broad middle. Explain why a panel that highlights only the base gives a misleading comparison.

answer.exemplar: A broad base means a high share of children, and a narrow base with a broad middle means an older age structure with many working-age people, but the base says nothing about how many elderly people each district must also support. Highlighting only the base therefore invites the reader to conclude that the district with more children has the heavier dependency burden, when the top of the pyramid could show the opposite once the older groups are counted.

questions.explanation: The base describes only the youngest groups, so comparing by base alone ignores the elderly who also depend on the working population. A real comparison needs the middle and top of each pyramid.
questions.hint: Ask what the top of the pyramid adds.

Zone West is denser, because the people are distributed across the whole area rather than clustered
options.misconception: reads wider spread as though it meant higher density

options.text: Zone East is denser, because compact settlements always hold more people per square kilometre
options.misconception: assumes compact form raises the measured density figure

options.text: The zones are identical, because the density tile reports the same figure for both
options.misconception: treats one matching tile as proof that the zones are alike

questions.explanation: The density tile is a ratio of people to area and cannot show pattern, so two zones can share a figure and differ in settlement form. West is linear and dispersed, East is compact and clustered.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the forces acting on a city population
questions.stem: A dashboard panel shows a city's population at 900,000 with a natural increase of 27,000 a year and a net migration balance of 9,000. First identify the two forces at work, then choose the correct reading.

options.text: One force at work, because births and deaths alone change the population in every city
options.misconception: denies that migration has any effect on the total

options.text: Two forces at work, but they cancel out, because 27,000 of natural increase meets 9,000 of net loss
options.misconception: adds the two forces with the wrong signs and calls it balance

options.text: Two forces at work, with natural increase of 27,000 and net migration of 9,000 adding to growth
Two forces at work, but net migration of 9,000 must be subtracted from natural increase
options.misconception: treats a positive migration balance as something to subtract

questions.explanation: Two forces change the total: natural increase of 27,000 and net migration of 9,000, adding 36,000 a year. Subtracting a positive migration balance, or treating them as cancelling, understates growth.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rate uses a population denominator
questions.stem: Why does a migration rate use the population as its denominator rather than the number of migrants?

options.text: Because the population figure is always larger and therefore makes the rate look smaller and safer
options.misconception: explains the choice by its effect on the size of the number

options.text: Because the number of migrants is hard to count and the population figure is easier to obtain
options.misconception: gives an administrative reason instead of the statistical one

options.text: Because the rate must measure migrants relative to the population they moved within
Because using the population as the denominator allows migrants to be compared across years
options.misconception: credits the denominator with a benefit it does not provide

questions.explanation: A rate expresses a flow relative to the population in which it occurred. Dividing by the number of migrants alone produces a ratio with no useful interpretation.

Village Two has the larger remittance share, because its remittance income is closer to 260,000
options.misconception: compares the absolute amounts rather than the shares

options.text: The villages are equal, because both receive remittances and neither relies on them entirely
options.misconception: treats both receiving transfers as making them equivalent

options.misconception: gives the right ranking for a reason that does not hold

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Remittances as a share of income
questions.learningObjective: Challenge a conclusion drawn from a remittance share
questions.stem: A development agency's dashboard reports that remittances supply 22 per cent of household income in one region, and a colleague argues the region is therefore economically dependent on transfers. Explain why that conclusion does not follow.

answer.exemplar: A share of income shows how large transfers are within a household budget, but it does not show that the money creates no local activity at all. Money sent home is typically spent on food, schooling, housing, and farm inputs, which circulate through local shops and suppliers and can support work that the income share conceals. The figure also says nothing about how the share has changed, or whether households could survive without it, so a single percentage cannot carry a conclusion about dependence.

questions.explanation: A share of income measures the size of transfers within a budget, not the absence of local activity. Received money is usually spent locally on shops and suppliers, so dependence cannot be concluded from it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the money is spent in the region.

questions.stem: Using the density panel, which conclusion about the island's population is best supported?

options.text: The island is thinly settled everywhere, because the territorial density of 61 is low
options.misconception: reads a low territorial density as evenly thin settlement

options.text: Most residents are concentrated in a small area, so the territorial density hides heavy local crowding
The island is densely settled everywhere, because most residents live in two settlements
options.misconception: generalises concentration into a claim about the whole territory

options.text: The territorial density figure is wrong, because most of the island is difficult terrain
options.misconception: dismisses the published figure instead of interpreting it

questions.explanation: A territorial density of 61 spreads people across land most residents never use, understating how crowded the inhabited part is. Putting 71 per cent of people in 9 per cent of the land is what the ratio conceals.

The population change itself, since movement is always the main reason a population changes
options.misconception: assumes movement dominates population change without evidence

options.text: The natural increase, since a balance tile must repeat the growth components for reference
options.misconception: fills the tile with a component rather than the balance

options.text: A blank value, because migration can never be inferred from counts of people
options.misconception: claims the balance can never be inferred from population counts

options.misconception: multiplies the rate by the population instead of dividing

questions.learningObjective: Interpret contrasting remittance shares
questions.stem: A district dashboard reports that remittances fund 34 per cent of household income in one upland district and 4 per cent in a nearby city. Explain what this contrast suggests about the two economies and what it does not tell you.

answer.exemplar: The upland district's much larger share suggests that transfers are a far more important part of the local economy than in the city, and that households there are more likely to depend on income earned elsewhere. It does not show that the upland district is poorer, since a high share of a small income can equal a low share of a large one, nor whether transfers are arriving because local work is scarce or because the district has strong family ties abroad.

questions.explanation: A larger share points to greater reliance on earnings from outside, but says nothing about absolute income levels or why transfers are sent. Different living standards can come with similar shares.
questions.hint: Ask what the percentage leaves out.

questions.stem: A dashboard team argues that their migration rate tile is wrong because the mid-year population is only an estimate, while a colleague points out that any denominator is an estimate. Explain what the sensible standard is for a published rate.

answer.exemplar: The mid-year population is an estimate, but it is the standard denominator precisely because it matches the period the flow was measured over, and replacing it with an equally uncertain count would not make the figure more reliable. What matters is that the definition is stated, so that a reader knows the denominator used and can compare with figures published on the same basis. The team's objection would improve nothing and would leave the tile without a consistent convention.

questions.explanation: The mid-year population matches the period of the flow, and swapping it for another estimate adds no accuracy. What matters is that the denominator and scale are stated so comparisons rest on a consistent basis.
questions.hint: Ask whether a different estimate would help.

questions.stem: A dashboard designer highlights the base of an age-sex pyramid for a policy audience. First identify what the base covers, then choose what the highlight would lead the audience to conclude wrongly.

options.text: The base covers children, so a wide base means the district carries a heavy dependency burden now
options.misconception: reads the youngest band as the entire dependent population

options.text: The base covers the oldest groups, so a narrow base means the district has no elderly dependants
options.misconception: misidentifies which ages the base of a pyramid represents

options.text: The base covers children, so a wide base says nothing about the elderly dependants the district also carries
The base covers all ages, so any highlight of it summarises the whole age structure
options.misconception: treats one band of the pyramid as the whole structure

questions.explanation: The base counts the youngest age groups only, so a wide base says nothing about the elderly, also dependants. The audience could infer a heavier dependency burden than the full pyramid supports.
questions.hint: Check which ages the base actually shows.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two density figures can both be valid
questions.stem: Why can two authorities publish different density figures for the same country without either being wrong?

options.text: Because one of them will have made a mistake in dividing the population by the area
options.misconception: assumes a difference of any kind must be an arithmetic error

options.text: Because density figures are revised every year, so older totals are always superseded
options.misconception: assumes the newest figure always replaces the earlier one

options.text: Because population figures are revised, so the older density is preferable for long-term series
options.misconception: invokes population revision to excuse an area-definition difference

options.text: Because each may use a different area definition, such as total land or habitable land

questions.explanation: Density depends on the area chosen, and a country with large uninhabited stretches has two defensible denominators. Publishing the area definition with each figure makes the difference explainable.
questions.hint: Ask what area each figure divided by.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Read a density figure against a map pattern
questions.stem: A county dashboard reports a density of 60 people per square kilometre across 5,200 square kilometres, while a map panel shows most households strung along a river valley and vast empty uplands. What is the correct reading?

options.text: The county is uniformly settled, because a density of 60 applies evenly across the whole area
options.misconception: treats an averaged ratio as a description of everywhere

options.text: 312,000 people concentrated in a valley, with the county average hiding an empty upland
312,000 people spread evenly, because the county's density figure describes the pattern
options.misconception: claims a ratio describes the distribution of people

options.text: 60 people live in the valley, because the dashboard's figure refers only to settled land
options.misconception: reverses the relationship between the ratio and the pattern

questions.explanation: The ratio implies 312,000 people across 5,200 square kilometres, but a single average cannot show that they occupy the valley while the uplands are empty. The map supplies the pattern that the density tile averages away.
questions.hint: Compute the implied total, then read the map.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain a flat total from offsetting components
questions.stem: A dashboard note shows a city whose population has been almost unchanged for fifteen years, with natural increase of 3 per cent a year and net migration of minus 3 per cent a year. Explain what this tells you about the city's population balance.

answer.exemplar: Natural increase and net migration are working in opposite directions at almost exactly the same strength, so the total barely moves even though both components are large. The city is not static: it is losing roughly the number of people that births and arrivals surplus, and the two rates are close enough that small changes in either would swing the total. The flat headline figure hides both an expanding natural balance and a substantial outflow.

questions.explanation: Two large and opposite components can cancel, so a flat total hides both strong natural increase and strong out-migration. Only reading the components separately shows what is happening.
questions.hint: Look at the components, not just the total.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Choosing a denominator for a migration rate
questions.learningObjective: Calculate an in-migration rate per thousand
questions.stem: A dashboard records 7,500 people arriving into a city during a year in which its mid-year population was 250,000. What is the in-migration rate per 1,000 residents?
questions.explanation: 7,500 over 250,000 is 0.03, and multiplying by 1,000 gives a rate of 30 per 1,000 residents. The same ratio expressed as a percentage is 3, so the scale of a published rate must always be stated.
questions.hint: Divide by the mid-year population and scale to a thousand.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a village dashboard note

stimulus.body: A village dashboard shows that the number of resident households fell from 610 to 480 between two counts, while total remittance receipts rose from 900,000 to 1,400,000 units. A note records that eleven households had relocated to the coast and that the village's clinic had opened in the period.

questions.stem: Using the village dashboard, which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: Fewer households but more transfers, consistent with out-migration sustained by money sent from those who left
The village gained population, because rising remittance receipts show more people are living there
options.misconception: reads rising transfers as proof of rising resident population

options.text: The clinic caused the fall in households, because new services always reduce the number of families
options.misconception: asserts a link between a clinic and household numbers with no evidence

options.text: Nothing can be inferred, because receipts and household counts are unrelated measures
options.misconception: claims the two measures cannot be related at all

questions.explanation: The fall of 130 households and the rise in transfers fit people leaving while sending money back, though the clinic is a competing factor. Receipts alone cannot show how many residents there are.
questions.hint: Ask what the two movements together could mean.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Remittances as a share of income
questions.learningObjective: Compute and interpret a remittance share
questions.stem: A dashboard reports a household's remittance income of 2,400 units and its total income of 9,600 units. First compute the share, then choose the correct interpretation.

options.text: The share is 25 per cent, and the household therefore depends entirely on money sent from elsewhere
options.misconception: treats a quarter of income as total dependence

options.text: The share is 40 per cent, because the remaining income of 7,200 is three times the transfer
options.misconception: divides the transfer by the remaining income instead of the total

options.text: The share is 25 per cent, so the transfer is important but most income is still earned locally
The share is 25 per cent, and the household is richer than one with a 30 per cent share
options.misconception: reads a lower share as proof of greater wealth

questions.explanation: Remittances of 2,400 in a total of 9,600 are one quarter, so 25 per cent. That is a meaningful contribution but not dependence, since 7,200 is earned locally, and a share says nothing about income levels.
questions.hint: Divide the transfer by the total income.
